steps.text: Part 3 of 3: Sure material, or a trap?. This part covers Mixed test; Real games and your words. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

**Mixed test.** From here nothing is labelled. Some positions offer sure material and taking it is the right move. Some hide a trap. One has nothing to take. Run the two questions each time, and do not treat every capture as a trap.

**What real players did** (Lichess games at 1100-1300; counts, not evaluations). Of 574 games where White's queen attacked the knight on e4, 51 retreated it to f6. Of 121 games reaching the pawn grab, 117 took it. After the f-pawn capture, 113 of 129 games recaptured with the pawn; the other 16 played something else. Of 430 games with the queen on g5, 166 chose the knight capture, and White scored 7.5% in those.

steps.text: **Recap.** A trap is a lure plus a hidden reply that your own capture made possible: an opened line, a counter-threat, a check in between, or a promotion. It works only while its pieces stand in place. Before a capture ask what it opens and which checks, captures and threats follow; if nothing, take. steps.prompt: Compare with a model answer. Idea: a trap is a lure that looks like a gain plus a hidden reply that your own capture made possible. When: the same capture works if no reply exists, and fails while the trap's pieces stand in place. Example: the first board of this lesson. Warning: before any capture, ask what it opens and which checks, captures and threats follow.

steps.text: **Remember.** A trap is a lure that looks like a gain plus a hidden reply your own capture allowed. Before a capture, ask what it opens and which checks, captures and threats follow. If nothing hurts, take the material. Not every capture is a trap, so do not fear them all.
